Question: When I merge a question I've answered into a question that I haven't answered, shouldn't my answer to the first show up as an answer on the second (and why doesn't it)?
Old_Answer: What actually happens is that the earlier question is the one into which the later one is merged. If you've answered both, the answer to the later one will normally be deleted. If you've answered one but not the other, your sole answer should show in the merged question. But recent mergers seem often to be showing as separate questions with related questions attached, and if that's what is happening, and you've answered the newer question, it may not be visible on the older one. This could be another of those unwanted Quora changes for no obvious reason!

When you merge a question, you're mostly just consolidating the questions themselves, not the answers associated with them. So, your brilliant answer might be left lonely and unremarked upon in the shadows of the original question while the new one doesn’t recognize it at all. It may sound silly, but think of it like trying to fit a square peg in a round hole; the system just doesn't accommodate those connections. If you really want your answer showcased, you might have to copy and paste it over manually or perhaps leave a comment on the new question directing others to your original insights. A bit of extra effort, but that's the nature of digital platforms, unfortunately!

Merging questions can sometimes change the focus or the audience's expectations, making it critical for answers to be specifically tailored to fit the new context. Additionally, managing content in this way helps prevent confusion among users; if answers were to appear across multiple questions without modification, it could dilute the clarity of responses and potentially mislead those seeking information. This structure encourages users to provide answers that directly address the person's query, fostering a higher quality of discussion on the platform. In essence, while it might seem logical for your previous answer to show up, the rules of content integrity and contextual appropriateness take precedence, ensuring that every response is relevant and tailored to the question it addresses.
Answer_with_full_information: When you merge a question you've answered into a question that you haven't addressed, it’s understandable to expect that your previous answer should automatically appear in the newly merged question. When merging, the original question's context can significantly influence the relevance and appropriateness of the answer. If the systems do not interpret the content of the two questions as closely related or if the keywords differ, they may decide not to carry over the previous answers to the new context. Additionally, it’s worth considering that answers can be very specific and tailored to the nuances of the original question, which may not perfectly align with the merged one. Question: What is the difference between O-levels/GCSEs and below O-levels/GCSEs? Which would I be if I was in year 10 and haven’t completed my GCSEs yet, but plan to?
Old_Answer: The big difference is that O levels (which originated in the UK, in the late 1940s) haven't existed here since 1988, though they survive in some countries. If you are in the UK, Year 10 is normally your first year of GCSE work, and you take the exams in Year 11. Year 10 doesn't mean the same here as it does in countries such as India, so there's room for confusion. If your family plans to go back to India partway through your GCSE courses, it will be complicated, because GCSE syllabuses aren't even all the same in the UK between different exam boards, and definitely not the same between countries, and between GCSE and O level. The standards should be very similar, but the content won't be. Try to stay in one place while doing your GCSEs, and your A levels.
Answer_with_writing_sample: If you haven’t completed your GCSEs yet and you're in Year 10, you're likely still working at a level below GCSEs, which often means you're either in the middle of your O-level equivalent courses or perhaps taking some foundation subjects. The system can be a bit convoluted, but simply put, GCSEs (General Certificate of Secondary Education) are the standard qualifications in the UK typically taken by students aged 14-16, while the term 'below' could refer to various levels of study, including lower-tier qualifications or ongoing assessments that lead to your eventual GCSEs. So, to answer your question, you're probably still in the learning phase, preparing to tackle those GCSEs soon. Don’t stress too much about labels; focus on mastering the material at your own pace, and before you know it, you'll be ready to take those exams and move up!
Answer_with_user_profile: O-levels (Ordinary Levels) and GCSEs (General Certificate of Secondary Education) are qualifications taken in the UK, typically by students around the age of 16. O-levels were phased out in the late 1980s and replaced by GCSEs, which have a broader curriculum and a different grading system. Whereas O-levels focused more on rote learning and were often graded A to E, GCSEs assess a wider range of skills, including coursework and practical assessments, and are graded from 9 to 1 (with 9 being the highest). If you are in year 10 and have not yet completed your GCSEs but plan to, you would be classified as a GCSE student, preparing to sit these exams usually in year 11. Below O-levels/GCSEs refers to any educational stage prior to these qualifications, including Key Stage 3, which encompasses years 7 to 9. This is where students typically age 11 to 14 build foundational knowledge and skills in various subjects. At this point, as you are still progressing through your education and aiming to achieve GCSEs, you are in a critical stage where you're preparing for these important qualifications that will influence your future educational and career pathways.
Answer_with_full_information: The distinction between O-levels/GCSEs and what precedes them is quite fundamental in the UK education system. O-levels, or Ordinary Levels, were the traditional examinations taken at the end of secondary education before GCSEs were introduced in the late 1980s as a more flexible and inclusive alternative. GCSEs, or General Certificates of Secondary Education, cover a broader range of subjects and offer varied assessment methods, including coursework and practicals, which aims to cater to different learning styles. If you are currently in Year 10 and have not yet completed your GCSEs, you're in the stage of preparation and study for them, which typically occurs in Years 10 and 11. At this point, you’re still working towards obtaining these qualifications, and it's often referred to as being 'on-course for your GCSEs.' Below O-levels/GCSEs would refer to qualifications like Lower Secondary education or earlier assessments that do not hold the same weight or recognition as GCSEs. In essence, you can think of yourself as a GCSE candidate, gearing up to sit these important exams, which are crucial for further education or vocational training afterward. Focus on doing your best, as success at the GCSE level opens up a multitude of pathways for your future education and career.

In the UK, children are still routinely taught it, and CIE is UK-based. Exam boards are moving towards having online exams word-processed, but as long as handwritten exam scripts are still being used, I very much doubt if there will be any problem with cursive script - which in any case is much faster than printing, just what you need in an exam. Don't worry unless you are explicitly instructed otherwise in an exam!

Honestly, focus on writing in a way that’s easy to follow. Unless you have the neat handwriting of a calligrapher, you might want to stick to a print style or at least make sure your cursive doesn’t look like a race against time. Question: Does lying require more effort?
Old_Answer: More effort than the truth? Definitely, if you want them to be believed. You've got to remember what lies you told, to whom. You'll probably also need to come up with other lies too, to try and cover up the obvious discrepancies between known facts and the story you've just been telling, all without hesitation, repetition or deviation, and then you'll have to remember those lies too. Elaborate fiction at short notice will have to be your strongest skill. If you fail in any of these, your lies will be immediately obvious to everyone around you. No-one will trust you, for good reason, and you'll quickly acquire a reputation for being a liar and a fool. As even Presidents and Princes have discovered, you can't fool all of the people all of the time. On balance, the truth, told at the right time rather than when it's dragged out of you, may be painful and embarrassing, but it's a whole lot easier, and in the long term, will involve much less pain and shame.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Yes, it generally does. Think about it: when you lie, you've not only got to create a fictional narrative, but also remember the details you've concocted. You have to keep track of your story and ensure it aligns with what you said before, otherwise you risk getting caught out. Meanwhile, telling the truth is straightforward; there's no mental gymnastics involved. Sure, being honest can be daunting at times, especially when you might hurt feelings, but you don't have to sweat over a lie falling apart. In a way, while lying may feel clever in the moment, it's really just a recipe for more stress in the long run. So, if you're trying to save energy, honesty is usually the less labor-intensive route!
Answer_with_user_profile: Yes, lying often requires more effort than telling the truth. When someone lies, they must not only fabricate a story but also remember the details to maintain consistency, which can become increasingly complex over time. This cognitive load arises from the need to manage the false narrative, monitor the reactions of others, and anticipate the possibility of being caught. Furthermore, liars may experience anxiety or guilt, which can heighten their emotional stress and complicate their interactions. In contrast, speaking the truth typically involves a simpler process of recalling actual events and feelings without the added burden of deception. Additionally, maintaining a lie might lead to further deceit if the initial lie necessitates additional falsehoods to cover for it, leading to a tangled web that becomes harder to untangle.
